findings.claim: Ofgem lists the main UK business electricity contract types: fixed-rate, variable-rate, deemed, out-of-contract, rollover/evergreen and flexible (structured). Suppliers may not offer all of them.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: fixed contracts fix unit rates and standing charges for the contract length, so the cost per kWh stays the same whatever happens to wholesale prices. Under a variable-rate contract the price can rise or fall during the contract, for example when wholesale prices change. Flexible (structured) contracts are 'suitable for large businesses that use a lot of energy' and let them buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better, instead of locking in one price.
findings.limitations: Ofgem's page gives only brief definitions. It doesn't set out pros and cons in detail, so the advantages and risks here are partly inferred from the definitions. The page shows no date. It doesn't mention 'pass-through' contracts by name. Ofgem only describes flexible/structured contracts as an option for large businesses.

findings.claim: Deemed and out-of-contract rates apply when no agreed contract is in place. They are usually the most expensive option and should generally be avoided or exited quickly.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you are put on a deemed contract automatically when you move into new premises without arranging a formal contract, or if your supplier goes out of business. Deemed rates are usually higher than negotiated rates. Out-of-contract rates apply when a fixed-term contract ends without a new deal, and are usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts. Some contracts roll over automatically, usually for 12 months, possibly at a higher rate. Citizens Advice: deemed tariffs are 'usually the most expensive tariffs', and you usually won't need to pay a fee or give notice to switch. A contract may include a roll-over period of no more than 12 months. Without one, or once it ends, you are on an out-of-contract tariff, which is 'usually very expensive'. You can switch at any time with no fee or notice. Suppliers should contact you about 3 months before a fixed term ends.
findings.limitations: Neither source gives actual deemed or out-of-contract rates. Rates are published by individual suppliers. The protections about roll-over periods and notice mainly relate to microbusinesses. Citizens Advice's advice applies to England.

findings.claim: Microbusinesses get extra protections, and the contract types and terms available depend on business size or consumption.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: a microbusiness has fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet total of no more than £2 million, or uses up to 100,000 kWh of electricity a year. Suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal prices before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Citizens Advice: a microbusiness on a fixed term should usually wait until the end to avoid an exit fee. Evergreen contracts may need up to 30 days' notice. Most business contracts last 1 to 3 years, and contracts agreed over the phone are binding. Most suppliers offer no cooling-off period.
findings.limitations: Thresholds are as stated on the Ofgem page, which shows no date, so they may change. Small and large business thresholds are on the Ofgem page but not repeated here.

findings.claim: Brokers and third-party intermediaries (TPIs) can arrange contracts. They are usually paid by supplier commission, and microbusinesses are entitled to commission disclosure. Brokers paid by suppliers must belong to a redress scheme.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you can arrange a contract yourself or use a broker, consultant or price comparison service. Brokers charge for their services. Some charge an upfront fee, but most are paid commission by the chosen supplier. Brokers paid by suppliers must be members of an approved redress scheme (Energy Ombudsman or the Utilities Intermediaries Association). Price comparison sites should be checked for commission and for how much of the market they cover. Citizens Advice: you might pay a one-off fee or pay through your energy costs. Brokers paid by the supplier must be registered with the Energy Ombudsman or UIA, and without registration you can't complain if something goes wrong. For microbusinesses, a broker paid by the supplier (a set amount or commission) must tell you how much the supplier pays before you agree a contract. Terms, including broker fees, should be sent within 10 days of agreeing. Customers can ask the supplier how the broker is paid. If a broker misled you, you may be able to cancel the contract or get your money back.
findings.limitations: The disclosure duty described applies to microbusinesses. Citizens Advice says the level of detail suppliers must give depends on business type, but that section is cut from the page text. Neither page quantifies typical commission levels. Ofgem's page doesn't say how disclosure works for larger businesses.

findings.claim: A UK business electricity price covers wholesale energy cost, network costs and environmental (government decarbonisation scheme) costs. Wholesale is typically about 40% of an electricity bill.
findings.evidence: Ofgem blog, 31 March 2026: the price 'covers a range of costs including the wholesale energy cost (the cost to buy energy), network costs (the infrastructure to transport energy), and environmental costs (government decarbonisation schemes). Typically, wholesale costs can be about 40% of your electricity bill and about 60% of your gas bill, but exact percentages will vary.' Prices vary by supplier and by the type and size of business. The blog says network costs were increasing in April (2026) to upgrade infrastructure, and that wholesale costs are volatile.
findings.limitations: The blog gives only a broad split and no full breakdown of a business bill. It doesn't name transmission versus distribution charges, or individual levies. Percentages are typical, not exact.

findings.claim: Bills have a variable consumption charge (unit rate) and a fixed standing charge. For VAT purposes the standing charge is treated as part of the electricity supply. Climate Change Levy is included in the value of the supply for VAT.
findings.evidence: HMRC VAT Notice 701/19: 'Gas and electricity bills include a variable consumption charge and a fixed standing charge.' Although shown separately on bills, the standing charge is regarded for VAT purposes as part of the charge for the supply. Where use is qualifying, the whole bill including the standing charge is reduced-rated. The notice also says 'The value of a supply for VAT purposes will include Climate Change Levy where appropriate.' Charges for use of transmission or distribution lines, transformers or meters, made without any supply of electricity, are always standard-rated.
findings.limitations: HMRC's notice is about VAT treatment, not a full commercial cost breakdown. The page extract is shortened, with gaps.

findings.claim: VAT: supplies of fuel and power are standard-rated unless they qualify for the reduced rate. Qualifying use includes domestic use, charity non-business use and small-scale use. HMRC records a temporary zero rate of VAT for Great Britain, announced 21 July 2026.
findings.evidence: VAT Notice 701/19 (last updated 28 October 2026): supplies are standard-rated unless eligible for the reduced rate under schedule 7A. Electricity not exceeding an average of 33 kilowatt hours per day (1,000 kilowatt hours per month) to one customer at one premises is reduced-rated (de minimis). Where 60% or more of a supply is qualifying use, the whole supply is treated as qualifying. Below 60%, the qualifying part is reduced-rated and the rest standard-rated. EV charging at publicly accessible points doesn't qualify for the de minimis. The page says: 'On 21 July 2026, the government announced a temporary zero rate of VAT for Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) for domestic supplies of electricity and other supplies of qualifying use.' Budget 2026 announced it would extend this zero rate by 3 months, from 31 March to 30 June 2027.
findings.limitations: The extract doesn't state the numeric standard or reduced rate, and refers readers elsewhere for the 'current rate of VAT'. The zero rate applies to qualifying use (such as domestic use), not ordinary commercial use, which remains standard-rated. Rates may change after 28 October 2026.

findings.claim: Climate Change Levy (CCL) main rates for electricity are £0.00775 per kWh from 1 April 2023, 2024 and 2025, £0.00801 per kWh from 1 April 2026 and £0.00827 per kWh from 1 April 2027. Climate change agreement holders get a 92% discount on electricity. Domestic and charity non-business supplies are outside the rates.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK/HMRC 'Climate Change Levy rates' (last updated 27 November 2025): the table gives electricity at 0.00775 for 1 April 2023, 2024 and 2025, 0.00801 from 1 April 2026 and 0.00827 from 1 April 2027 (£ per kWh). Climate change agreement holders get a 92% discount on electricity throughout. 'The rates do not apply to taxable commodities supplied to domestic consumers and charities for non-business use.' Suppliers are responsible for charging the correct levy to customers. Carbon Price Support is charged on generators at £0.00331 per kWh for gas, from 1 April 2016 to 31 March 2028.
findings.limitations: The page doesn't list other CCL exemptions. It also doesn't say whether CCL is passed through in fixed contracts.

findings.claim: Supplier contracts: Ofgem says fixed contracts fix unit rates and standing charges for the term, while variable contracts can change with wholesale prices. Ofgem and Citizens Advice don't detail which non-commodity charges are fixed versus passed through.
findings.evidence: Ofgem (S1): fixed rate contracts fix 'the price of unit rates and standing charges for the length of the contract'. Variable-rate prices can rise or fall during the contract. Ofgem advises checking what fees and charges are involved and whether broker commission is in the price. The Ofgem blog (S4) notes that businesses should check terms before contracting.
findings.limitations: Not answered: no official source read says which non-commodity charges (network, policy levies, CCL) are fixed or passed through in fixed versus pass-through contracts. Pass-through contracts are not described by Ofgem beyond 'flexible'. This needs industry or supplier sources.

findings.claim: Microbusinesses get extra contract protections. The Ofgem microbusiness definition covers use below 100,000 kWh of electricity a year, or fewer than 10 employees and turnover not above 2 million euros. Small businesses are defined separately.
findings.evidence: Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): 'A Micro Business consumer uses less than 100,000 kWh of electricity a year; uses less than 293,000 kWh of gas a year; or has fewer than 10 employees (or their full-time equivalent) and an annual turnover total not exceeding 2 million Euros (equivalent to £1.716m according on 22 March 2024).' Small Business: fewer than 50 employees and turnover of £6.5 million or balance sheet total of £5 million, or annual electricity use of 200,000kWh or gas use of 500,000 kWh. Ofgem's current business contract page (S1) says microbusinesses are entitled to clear contract information and renewal prices before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Citizens Advice (S2): a roll-over period can't exceed 12 months. Suppliers should contact customers about 3 months before a fixed term ends. Once the fixed term has ended, you can switch with no fee or notice. A deemed tariff also needs no fee or notice to switch. An exit fee may apply if you leave a fixed term early.
findings.limitations: Definitions differ slightly between sources (Ofgem's current page gives a 'no more than £2 million' turnover test, the 2024 release gives 2 million euros). Notice, rollover and renewal protections are described by Ofgem and Citizens Advice mainly for microbusinesses and evergreen contracts. The primary licence conditions (SLC 7A etc.) weren't read, and neither were the rules covering larger businesses' contract terms.

findings.claim: Ofgem extended the Standards of Conduct to all non-domestic customers from 1 July 2024 and tightened rules on broker fee transparency, complaints signposting and TPI redress.
findings.evidence: Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): from 1 July 2024 Ofgem will 'Expand the Standards of Conduct to apply to all businesses of any size, rather than just Micro Business consumers', giving powers to act against suppliers that don't treat non-domestic customers fairly. A new supply licence rule requires suppliers to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice and Citizens Advice Scotland, and for Small Business consumers from December 2024. The requirement for a contract's principal terms to clearly display broker fees was expanded from microbusinesses to all non-domestic customers, for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024, and suppliers must make the information available on request. From December 2024 Ofgem would update Complaints Handling Standards for Small Business consumers, pointing them to the Energy Ombudsman. Suppliers must work only with TPIs that are members of a redress scheme when securing Small Business contracts. Redress schemes named are the Energy Ombudsman and the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA).
findings.limitations: This is an April 2024 announcement of planned rules. Some dates were described as 'expected' or subject to legislation, so the final licence text and effective dates should be checked. Later changes after April 2024 are not covered, other than the Ombudsman's later page.

findings.claim: Redress route: complain to the supplier first. The Energy Ombudsman can take small business disputes after deadlock or eight weeks, can award up to £20,000, and can't fine suppliers or set prices.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman page (last updated 13 April 2026): you should first raise the issue with your supplier. If you reach 'deadlock', or the supplier has taken more than eight weeks to consider the complaint, you can ask the Ombudsman to help. From 19 December 2024 small businesses became eligible: fewer than 50 employees and turnover of at most £6.5 million or balance sheet total of £5.0 million, or electricity use of not more than 200,000 kWh, or gas use of not more than 500,000 kWh. Common disputes concern billing, sales process, customer service, switching problems and charges. Outcomes include practical action, an apology, financial awards up to £20,000 and recommendations. It can't punish suppliers, dictate how they operate or issue fines. The page notes that 'We don't set the price of gas or electricity', although it may help if you were charged incorrectly or mis-advised. It can't deal with commercial decisions about whether to provide a product or service, or with LPG. After a decision the supplier has 28 days to implement the remedy. The maximum award for brokers differs. Citizens Advice (S2) says a business can complain to its supplier or broker, and a misled customer may be able to cancel a contract or get money back.
findings.limitations: Page is about supplier disputes. Broker disputes are on a separate Ombudsman page that wasn't opened, so the broker award limit isn't stated. Larger businesses beyond the small business definition fall outside this scheme, and this source doesn't say what redress they have.

findings.claim: Ofgem's practical guidance for businesses: no cooling-off period, suppliers aren't obliged to offer a contract, deposits may be required, and get contracts in writing.
findings.evidence: Ofgem blog (31 March 2026): suppliers 'may require security deposits'; 'energy suppliers are not obliged to offer businesses a contract'; there is no cooling off period, so check terms and fees beforehand; ask for phone contracts in writing; verify unexpected calls. Ofgem says suppliers must treat customers fairly and bill accurately, and it points to the Energy Ombudsman for supplier disputes and to a broker's redress provider for broker disputes. It says it expects 10-12% of businesses to be on deemed contracts. Staying temporarily on deemed or out-of-contract rates may be better if longer-term offers are high. Ofgem's contract page (S1) likewise says there is no cooling-off period after agreeing a contract and that brokers paid by suppliers must belong to an approved redress scheme.
findings.limitations: Guidance and context from March 2026 about market conditions, not formal rules. The 10-12% figure is Ofgem's expectation at that date.

findings.claim: Before signing, check the current contract's end date, term, notice rules and what happens at the end (rollover, out-of-contract or deemed rates). Compare quotes like for like on unit rate, standing charge, term, fees and exit terms.
findings.evidence: Ofgem (S1): before agreeing, know the contract type, term length, any fees (for example special clauses), your protections, and whether broker fees or commissions are in the price. Also know what happens at the end, including automatic renewal or a move to out-of-contract or deemed rates. Citizens Advice (S2): check the current contract's terms including the end date, standing charges and per-unit costs, and annual usage. When comparing, check the unit price and whether it can change, extra costs such as maintenance charges, contract length and any cancellation fee, the notice needed to end it, and whether there is a cooling-off period (most suppliers offer none). Most business contracts last between 1 and 3 years. Negotiate and mention other offers. Ask for the full terms and conditions and a written contract, since contracts agreed over the phone are binding.
findings.limitations: Neither page gives a formal checklist for meter type or MPAN. Citizens Advice's advice is for England and written for small businesses. Both pages show no date.

findings.claim: Supplier credit and deposits: Ofgem warns that suppliers may require security deposits, may not offer contracts, and that businesses should not be rushed. It also advises considering short-term options in volatile markets.
findings.evidence: Ofgem blog, 31 March 2026 (S4): 'suppliers may require security deposits because of greater risks of businesses defaulting on payment'; 'energy suppliers are not obliged to offer businesses a contract and offers may be harder to find'; you shouldn't feel pressured, and there is no cooling off period; ask for phone contracts in writing and verify unexpected callers to avoid fraud. 'It may be better for you to temporarily stay on deemed or out of contract rates if the current longer-term contract offers are high.' Ask suppliers about both short and long-term options. Submit regular meter readings or get a smart meter to be billed accurately. Citizens Advice (S2): if your supplier goes bust, don't switch tariff or supplier until your account has moved to the new supplier.
findings.limitations: No source read explains how credit checks are done or how deposit amounts are set. Supplier financial stability checks are not covered, apart from the Citizens Advice warning about supplier failure.

findings.claim: Checking brokers: use brokers that belong to a redress scheme, ask how they're paid, and avoid clauses recovering 'lost' commission. Brokers are not licensed by Ofgem.
findings.evidence: Ofgem (S1): brokers charge, mostly by supplier-paid commission. Brokers paid by suppliers must belong to an approved redress scheme (check the Energy Ombudsman broker register or the UIA accredited member list). There is no cooling-off period, so use a trustworthy broker. Citizens Advice (S2): check the broker's registration before agreeing. Without it you can't complain if something goes wrong. A broker paid by the supplier must tell a microbusiness how much before it agrees, and terms should arrive within 10 days. UIA consumer guidance (S8, updated 28 August 2026): TPIs 'are not licensed'. Confirm the TPI is UIA-accredited and follows its Code of Practice, and is in a Broker ADR scheme if you are a micro or small business. Ask how the TPI is paid. Be cautious of 'free' services, because costs may be in energy rates. Confirm all charges before signing. Request termination fees, price changes, notice periods and duration. Avoid TPIs whose contracts let them recover 'lost' commissions if contracts don't go live or end early. Verbal contracts are binding, so consider recording calls. The UIA says it has run a Code of Practice and Redress Scheme since 2006. Register with the Corporate Telephone Preference Service to cut unsolicited calls.
findings.limitations: S8 is a trade body (the UIA, which accredits brokers) and is not a regulator, so its advice is industry self-regulatory guidance. Wider code-of-practice coverage among brokers was not examined.

findings.claim: Microbusiness protections relevant when signing, according to the UIA: back-billing limit, 10-day contract provision, rollover cap, renewal notice and broker fee disclosure.
findings.evidence: UIA guidance (S8) lists these microbusiness protections: suppliers cannot charge for energy consumed over 12 months ago if incorrectly billed. Principal terms, including broker fees, must be clearly disclosed. Full contract terms are due within 10 days of signing. Automatic rollovers are limited to a maximum of 12 months. Suppliers can't require switching notice except for evergreen contracts. Suppliers must provide key renewal terms at least 60 days before expiry. The page also says new business premises are on expensive deemed rates, so take time to research suppliers rather than rushing into long-term contracts. Take regular meter readings if you rely on manual readings.
findings.limitations: Summarised by a trade body, not by Ofgem or legislation, and not independently checked against licence conditions. Other sources describe the renewal information duties differently, or without a stated day count.

findings.claim: ESOS is a mandatory energy assessment scheme for large UK undertakings. For phase 4 the qualification date is 31 December 2026 and the notification deadline is 5 December 2027. Qualifying organisations must assess every 4 years.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK ESOS guidance (last updated 2 September 2026): organisations that qualify 'must carry out an assessment every 4 years', covering energy used by buildings, industrial processes and transport. A large undertaking is a UK company that employs 250 or more people, or has annual turnover above £44 million and a balance sheet total above £38 million. Phase 4 changes: Display Energy Certificates and Green Deal assessments can no longer be used as alternative compliance routes, progress against action plan commitments must be reported, and unmet commitments must be explained. Net zero considerations can be added voluntarily using BSI PAS 51215 standards. The regulator can issue civil sanctions including financial penalties. ISO 50001 is an alternative compliance route.
findings.limitations: Covers ESOS only. SECR, Energy Intensive Industries support and other schemes were not found in sources read. The exact penalty amounts were not shown. The page text is shortened.

findings.claim: Green tariff claims are substantiated through REGOs. A REGO is issued per MWh of eligible renewable output and supports suppliers' Fuel Mix Disclosure.
findings.evidence: Ofgem REGO page: 'One REGO certificate is issued per megawatt hour (MWh) of eligible renewable output to generators of renewable electricity.' The REGO scheme 'provides transparency to consumers about the proportion of electricity that suppliers source from renewable electricity.' The primary use is Fuel Mix Disclosure, which requires licensed suppliers to disclose the mix of fuels (coal, gas, nuclear, renewable and other) used to generate the electricity supplied. Ofgem administers the scheme for Great Britain on behalf of DESNZ. EU Guarantees of Origin are no longer recognised for GB Fuel Mix Disclosure from the disclosure period beginning 1 April 2023, and the EU no longer recognises UK REGOs as of 1 January 2021.
findings.limitations: Ofgem's page shows no date. It describes REGOs and Fuel Mix Disclosure at a high level and doesn't explain how a business should verify a supplier's specific green tariff claim, or the difference between REGO-backed and PPA-backed supply.

findings.claim: Non-domestic smart meters: suppliers had binding rollout targets to the end of 2025, and 'smart-contingent contracts' are now used to drive uptake. DESNZ consulted on a post-2025 framework, with requirements from 2027.
findings.evidence: DESNZ consultation (issued 23 October 2025; page last updated 1 September 2026): the existing targets framework required 68.7% of relevant non-domestic premises to have smart meters by the end of 2025, when it ends. 64% of smaller non-domestic sites had smart or advanced meters at end Q2 2025. The rollout covers ~3 million meters in smaller-medium sites. Smart-contingent contracts are fixed-term contracts requiring a smart or advanced meter, and the government says fixed term contracts of this type are typically around 40% cheaper than deemed and out-of-contract rates. Suppliers are under no obligation to supply premises when requested. The consultation considers a requirement that suppliers can't enter new fixed term contracts unless the customer has, or agrees to, smart or advanced meters, with information to consumers 'from 2027'. It asks whether to extend this to larger sites (profile classes 5-8, or gas above 732 MWh a year), where suppliers must currently supply advanced meters subject to all reasonable steps. Smart meters are expected to reduce consumption by between 2.8% (electricity) and 4.5% (gas) per non-domestic meter. Since 1 October 2024, suppliers must give smaller organisations with smart meters free regular energy use information. Organisations of all sizes can request free access to their smart meter data (since 1 December 2022).
findings.limitations: This is a consultation, so proposals may have changed. Final rules were not confirmed in the page. The page text was shortened. Applies to Great Britain.

findings.claim: Market volatility and purchasing strategy: Ofgem notes wholesale volatility and longer contract lengths, and describes flexible contracts as a way to buy in portions. The recontracting timing choices can matter.
findings.evidence: Ofgem blog, 31 March 2026 (S4): wholesale energy costs are volatile and 'will continue to be affected by the situation in the Middle East'. Network costs were increasing in April. Contract lengths were 'starting to return to 3 to 5 years in length'. Ofgem expected less than 10% of businesses to recontract in March and April, with 10-12% on deemed contracts and another 10% likely to recontract in May to July. It says it may be better to temporarily stay on deemed or out-of-contract rates if longer-term offers are high, and to consider short and long-term options. Ofgem's contract page (S1): flexible (structured) contracts suit large businesses and let them buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better, instead of locking in at one price. Fixed contracts keep the cost per kWh the same whatever wholesale prices do. Variable contracts can rise or fall. The blog also mentions business energy efficiency grants and schemes, and that a business may be eligible for financial assistance.
findings.limitations: Ofgem's commentary is general and time-specific (March 2026). It doesn't give a formal purchasing strategy such as layered or block buying. The temporary deemed-rate suggestion is not advice for every business.

findings.claim: VAT and CCL reliefs available to some electricity buyers: reduced VAT for qualifying use, and reduced CCL for climate change agreement holders.
findings.evidence: VAT Notice 701/19 (S5, updated 28 October 2026): qualifying use, including domestic use and charity non-business use, is reduced-rated. Small-scale supplies up to an average of 33 kilowatt hours per day (1,000 kilowatt hours per month) are reduced-rated under the de minimis. Supplies with 60% or more qualifying use are wholly reduced-rated.
